newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore oil refiners rush to cut runs amid losses.
newsitem.headline: Singapore oil refiners rush to cut runs amid losses.

text.p: Singapore refiners have started a series of production cuts as plunging oil product prices turn profits negative, industry sources said on Monday.

Refinery sources told Reuters they were losing up to $1.50 a barrel on processing crude into products. This primary refining margin, or the first stage of processing crude, has come down by almost $2.00 in the past week.
"It's negative almost across the board on sweet and sour (crudes)," one crude trading manager said of refining margins. "There is only a handful of crudes that make a margin."
Returns from secondary refining units, which process residue fuel into lighter and more valuable products, ranged between a loss of 50 cents to a gain of $1.50 per barrel, they said.
In an almost knee-jerk reaction to sudden losses, three of Singapore's four refineries made immediate cuts or plans to reduce crude throughputs.
Shell Singapore took the lead and on Friday announced it had cut runs for an indefinite period at its 435,000 barrel-per-day (bpd) refinery by 4,000 tonnes per day (30,000-bpd).
Esso Singapore on Monday said it started cutting runs over the weekend at its 230,000-bpd refinery by 20 to 25 percent.

Meanwhile, a source said the Singapore Refining Co (SRC) would take advantage of a delay in crude cargo delivery due in early February, and cut its current production of 280,000-bpd by 10,000 to 15,000-bpd within the week for up to fifteen days.
"We can swap the delayed cargo or buy the crude on the spot market but because of the (profit) margins, we don't want to explore that option," said the source.

SRC is 40-percent owned by Singapore Petroleum Co. The remaining stake in the company is equally shared between British Petroleum & Co Plc and Caltex Group of Companies. Caltex is a joint-venture between Chevron Corp and Texaco Inc.
The fourth refiner in Singapore, Mobil Oil Singapore was also considering cutting output at its 280,000-bpd facility, company sources told Reuters.
Mobil and SRC have scheduled refinery shutdowns in March. But sources from both companies said these were too far forward to affect the decision to reduce throughputs.
"If middle distillates don't pick up or crude does not come off in a big way, it (cuts) will be here for some time, which in the middle of winter is dreadful," said a crude trading manager.
Traders said although weaker oil product prices across the barrel were responsible for the losses, diesel suffered the greatest fall, crashing nearly $4.00 per barrel last week.
"It is not just a matter of margins turning negative," said a middle distillate trader with a major U.S. oil company.
"Refinery margins are a paper situation," he complained. "The physical situation is more depressing. The physical is stagnant and Singapore barrels are backing up."
Traders were bearish on the immediate outlook as China, the main outlet for diesel, would take a pause for two weeks during the Lunar New Year in early February.

"If refinery cuts are long enough, that is, (they) continue for two to three weeks, no arbitrage cargoes arrive and good Indian demand stops Mideast cargoes from coming here, you might see an improvement in gas oil (diesel) prices and margins," a trader said.
